Q573619.summary: The Virgin, dark-faced and grave, holds the Christ Child on her left arm and gestures towards him, in the ancient Hodegetria ('she who shows the way') pattern; the Child raises his right hand in blessing and holds a book of the Gospels. Her blue mantle is scattered with gold fleurs-de-lis, and two parallel scars cut across her right cheek. A fifteenth-century legend says the panel was painted by St Luke on a tabletop from the house of the Holy Family; art historians instead date the present painting to the Middle Ages. Enshrined at Jasna Góra since the 1380s, it is the most venerated image in Poland, honoured as Queen of Poland.
facts: The oldest written account of its history, the fifteenth-century Translatio tabulae, describes it as the panel 'which St Luke painted with his own hands'; tradition dates its arrival at Jasna Góra to 1384.
Robbers slashed and broke the image in 1430; it was restored in Kraków in 1430–1434, and the scars on the Virgin's cheek were then deliberately incised and emphasised in memory of the attack.

Proposed dates range from the 7th to the 14th century; a 1984 analysis by Anna Różycka-Bryzek and Jerzy Gadomski found three layers — an icon-like first layer (12th–13th century), the present Italian paint layer (mid-14th century or later) and the 1430s repainting.
Q573619.notes: The previous 'c' value ('Jerusalem') reproduced the St Luke legend as fact and has been replaced. Dating remains disputed (English Wikipedia reports a 6th–9th-century Byzantine original); the date given follows the 1984 technical study and the Polish scholarship summarised on pl.wikipedia. The image file is a scan from W. Kurpik, Częstochowska Hodegetria (2008), showing the panel without its votive dresses.

cur:catacombs-sarcophagus-31537.summary: A continuous frieze of tightly packed figures runs across the front: Christ performs miracles among the apostles, and at the right end he rides on a donkey into Jerusalem while a man spreads his garment before him. The relief reads like a pageant of Christ's saving works culminating in his royal entry.
facts: Commons records that the sarcophagus comes from the Coemeterium Maius on the Via Nomentana.
Continuous frieze sarcophagi of this kind were the commonest type of Christian sarcophagus in Constantinian Rome.

cur:objects2-seal-symeon-seleucia.summary: The Theotokos stands frontally in chiton and maphorion, holding on her left arm the Christ Child, who wears tunic and mantle and holds a scroll; cruciform invocation monograms flank the figure. The reverse gives the name of Symeon, metropolitan of Seleucia. Struck around 800, in the very decades of the iconoclast controversy, the seal shows a bishop who chose the image of the incarnate Christ with his Mother as his personal emblem.
facts: The Commons record dates the seal to Symeon's tenure, c. 787–815, beginning in the year of the Second Council of Nicaea, which restored the veneration of icons.
Seleucia (modern Silifke in southern Turkey) was the metropolitan see of the province of Isauria.

wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/2ravenna/5vitale/2.summary: In the golden apse of San Vitale, a youthful, beardless Christ in purple sits upon a blue sphere representing the cosmos, with the four rivers of Paradise flowing beneath him. Flanked by two angels, he holds out a jeweled crown of martyrdom to St. Vitalis, while Bishop Ecclesius, the church's founder, offers him a model of the building. The serene, eternal figure presides over the famous imperial panels of Justinian and Theodora below.
facts: In his left hand Christ holds a scroll sealed with seven seals, recalling the Book of Revelation.
The church was begun under Bishop Ecclesius in 526, financed by the banker Julius Argentarius, and completed and consecrated under Bishop Maximian in 547.
The youthful Christ in the apse contrasts with the bearded Christ in the medallion at the crown of the triumphal arch, showing both types side by side in one building.
San Vitale is the only major church of Justinian's era to survive virtually intact, and its mosaics are among the largest and best-preserved Byzantine mosaics outside Istanbul.
